draft_context.source_title: New York Governor Kathy Hochul thinks AI should be ‘less evil’
draft_context.description: Today, I’m talking with New York Governor Kathy Hochul, and I’ll just warn you — this episode moves really fast. It’s an election year, after all, with a shocking amount of tech policy at stake, and Governor Hochul has taken strong positions on almost every major tech issue there is. For example, Meta just reached a settlement with dozens of states, including New York, which will restrict how teens use platforms like Instagram in very specific ways. Governor Hochul is a strong supporter of those restrictions and more, as you’ll hear. But those come with a cost — widespread age verification means adults will also have to show ID to use the internet, which will essentially make it impossible to be anonymous online. Verge subscribers, don’t forget you get exclusive access to ad-free Decoder wherever you get your podcasts. Head here . Not a subscriber? You can sign up here . So I asked about that, and if these new restrictions amount to Meta conceding in a lawsuit that these kinds of regulations on speech might not pass First Amendment scrutiny if the governor were to try and impose them in a law. I had similar questions about New York’s restrictions on ghost guns, which prevent 3D printers from printing gun parts. That law is already being challenged — not in courts, but by activists like Cody Wilson, who runs the largest database of 3D-printable gun files and who has started altering those files in a process he calls “Hochulization” in order to show the ban is technically toothless. I asked the governor about this, and, well, you’ll hear her challenge Cody right back. Oh, but there’s more: We also talked about surveillance and Flock cameras, and, of course, the politics of AI and data centers in an election year. Governor Hochul signed a one-year moratorium on data center construction in July, and I wanted to know what she’s looking for when that expires to make data centers a workable proposition. We also talked a little about Mayor Zohran Mamdani in New York City and, of course, her org chart for the state government. This one is a lot, I think you’re going to like it. Okay: New York Governor Kathy Hochul, here we go. This interview has been lightly edited for length and clarity. Governor Kathy Hochul, you are the governor of the state of New York! Welcome to Decoder . Thank you. Happy to be on. I have so much to talk to you about. We don’t have a ton of time, so we’re going to move fast. Are you up for it? I’m up. All right. I want to start with what I call the Decoder questions, lightning round style. I think the operation of your office and state government is really opaque to most people. So I ask everybody this question. How is the governor’s office structured? How did you make decisions about how to structure that office? How did you organize it? Governor at the top. Then there’s a leadership team, senior leadership team. There’s a secretary to the governor who is the top advisor. It sounds like the person taking notes at meetings, but the secretary of the governor is the most powerful non-elected position in the state. When I first became governor five years ago, I said, “I want the smartest, the best, the brightest people I could surround myself with.” I didn’t know a lot of these individuals, but they were highly recommended from having business experience, government experience, or technological experience. I said, “Bring me the smartest.” There’s a layer of senior team members. There’s one individual who oversees all the agencies. There are 45 different agencies for everything from the Department of Transportation to the environment to our housing development agency, economic development. It all trickles down to a pretty large bureaucracy. I’m the decision maker, but I take input from a lot of different levels of government before I make a final decision. But I’m a fairly quick decision-maker. Show me the facts and I can make a decision instantaneously. You took over in a complicated way from your predecessor and then you won reelection. Did you sit down and make an org chart of how you wanted your office to work? Yes, I did. How long did that take? I inherited one in a sense, but also early on I didn’t have a lot of tools. In fact, we had a hurricane in my first week. I didn’t know how to declare a disaster. I hadn’t hired that person yet, the head of emergency services. We were caught off-guard a little bit. The state still functioned, but I knew I needed to do more. I’m always in search of talent, smart people, and trying to rotate people in. Sometimes I start commissions like the Future Works Commission to bring in experts, not just from my administration but around the country, who understand the displacement of jobs because of AI: who’s most vulnerable, how we deal with that, and how we train people to be able to overcome those obstacles or to embrace AI as a possible career. I’m always finding ways to supplement my team with industry- or issue-specific experts. This question’s going to sound ridiculous, but I’ve asked a lot of people a variation of this question. Almost no one ever is going to sit down and say, “I need to write a new org chart for the governor’s office of New York.” Did you do that on a whiteboard? Did you open PowerPoint? Was it just you alone with a laptop? What was it actually like? Can I tell you something I’m embarrassed of, since you phrased it that way? I did it on a legal pad. Nice. Old school. Sorry. Yeah, pen and paper. No, it’s great. Very few people do that. You would be surprised at some of the answers we’ve gotten to questions like that. I just laid out, “This is what I need, this is the team I need.” Now that was five years ago. I’ve gotten a little better. I’d probably ask Claude or ChatGPT for some recommendations. Oh boy. We’re going to come to that. Don’t worry about it. You started answering this question, but this is the other Decoder question. How do you make decisions? What’s your framework? Bring in all the information as quickly as possible, pressure-test it, and then go with my gut. One of the more unique parts about structure in New York government is the relationship between the state and the city. We’re talking here in person in New York City. Mayor Zohran Mamdani has been pretty aggressive about going after billionaires and tech companies. Most recently the city went after Amazon for its labor practices. Do you think that’s been effective here? I need to make sure that New York City and the state overall continue to be a place where we support innovation, new jobs. Technology is leading the forefront right now. I’m really proud that we now have been named the number-one job creator for tech jobs in the country, surpassing California, which has always dominated in this space. That says something about our ecosystem and I want to foster that. I want people who have just an idea who can use technology to create something that no one else had ever conceived of and be successful in marketing it. That is what I’m leaning hard into. The mayor has his own approach, but I think overall we both want New York City to succeed. To me, success also means creating more opportunities for jobs because of the spinoff effect. Five guys in an office right in this building could lead to 500 jobs in a couple of years. Those opportunities help lift people out of their circumstances and achieve what I’m hoping for is more opportunity for more people. There’s a WeWork just above us. We got to go find those five guys. I’m asking specifically about the more aggressive approach the mayor has taken. He’s taken a very aggressive approach. And like you said, the numbers show that the billionaires didn’t run, they’re actually investing; the tech companies didn’t run, they’re actually hiring at a rate that surpasses San Francisco. Is that emboldening you to take a harsher regulatory approach to tech companies? I don’t just take a regulatory approach for the sake of doing it. I don’t raise taxes for the sake of doing it. I do things in a smart way when it’s necessary. For example, we have regulations on tech companies when it comes to social media for young people under the age of 18. My job is to protect the young people of our state because they have been spiraling with mental health challenges — exacerbated by the pandemic, yes, but many of them have not overcome that sense of doom and anxiety. It is pervasive in our teenagers particularly. I look at my role to regulate tech companies in that space. Before the Meta settlement, we had innovated and come up with probably three years’ worth of reforms to force the companies to do things that they are otherwise not doing on their own, and one would wish they would but that’s probably being too optimistic. We have in place, for example, no notifications to someone under the age of 18 between midnight and 6:00 AM. These kids need to sleep. We’re saying addictive algorithms can no longer bombard young people, having — this is a big deal — automatic privacy controls that are already set. Parents aren’t expected to understand every platform where their kids may go or any gaming site and have to get ahead of them. That it’s automatic using age verification is really important. Limiting access to AI chatbots for young people and making sure there are disclaimers so they understand this is not a real person that you think you’re having a relationship with: that’s an example where I think tech needs to be regulated. It went out of control and now the government has to perform a function to protect our residents and our young people, the most vulnerable. I don’t just regulate to stifle their growth. I want them to grow. It’s a smart, strategic, more surgical approach to regulations. I’m glad you brought up the Meta settlement. That’s obviously the big news this week. Meta settled with 47 states , including New York. I look at that settlement, I look at the list of controls that Meta has agreed to and my initial reaction was this is a bunch of stuff that, if passed as a law, would run into the teeth of the First Amendment. They are effectively speech restrictions, right? We’re going to prevent young people from using these platforms to speak at certain hours of the day. And maybe there’s some argument that overcomes the First Amendment objection, right? The teen health risk is so high that this is actually a narrowly crafted, strict scrutiny-abiding restriction, but we don’t know that. That actually hasn’t been challenged in court. Meta just gave that to you. Then there’s age verification to prove that you’re over 18. Even if you’re an adult, you still have to show the internet your ID, which is a big ask for people who are not covered by the restrictions. That’s a big swirl. Do you think you got concessions from Meta that you otherwise would not have been able to get if you just passed the law? No, we actually have laws in New York that are more restrictive than some of what Meta has agreed to. Are you worried about the First Amendment implications of some of those laws? No, I’m not. And here’s why: we have an opportunity and the responsibility to protect our residents. The First Amendment is when the government says that we’re limiting your speech. Not having notifications that keep you awake all night when you’re a 13-year-old is not restricting your First Amendment right to free speech. There is a difference. Sometimes the First Amendment is used as any kind of government regulation. People will say, “Oh my God, you’re violating the First Amendment” or any of the other amendments. I’m an attorney. I look at it closely. I don’t do things to violate amendments or any laws. It’s not my practice. We’re smart about how we structure these and make sure that we’re protecting First Amendment rights as well as protecting young people from having their mental health monetized by companies who have a profit motive. It’s almost like cigarette smoking. The earlier you get them, the longer you’re going to keep them hooked. Young people should not be bombarded with the addictive algorithms or be subjected to the bullying that goes on. Someone who’s thinking about suicide searches for “suicide” and is now told different ways to commit suicide. That is terrifying for parents. Parents actually appreciate the fact that they have a voice in government. Maybe it’s because I’m the first mom governor in New York that I understand this. I’ve raised kids. I know the pressures they’re under. Something else we did: I’m really proud of the fact that we’re the biggest state in the nation to have come up with a full ban on cell phones in schools. Now you can say it’s violating their First Amendment rights. I’m saying I’m protecting them from a lifetime of addiction to a device where they no longer have human relationships. You asked how I make decisions. Sometimes I go with my gut, sometimes I want confirmation from the real world and I go out there and talk to people in schools and in cafeterias and have a lot of conversations with young people. When I did round tables around the state of New York for about a solid year to get information, [students] were so anxious about missing a notification. “The girls are meeting in the restroom to plan activities for Friday night and I just got excluded and I’m also getting knocked out because of what I’m wearing. And now they’ve got a picture of me in an inappropriate way being sent around the school.” These kids are paralyzed. One young person, probably a sixth grader, said to me, “You’ve got to save us from ourselves. We can’t put these down. We’ll be ostracized.” That’s when I took it to heart and I said, “I will protect you. I’ll protect these kids.” We literally instituted this in September. The survey results from just this past May show anywhere from 75% to 80% of the schools surveyed have been overwhelmingly positive. The kids who resisted at first are now making friends in person. There’s more communication. They’re learning the interpersonal skills that you’d want your future workforce to have, and they’re playing games at lunchtime. They’re playing cards. They have baseball cards they’re trading. They’re playing chess, bingo. It’s almost silly, but they’re just being kids again. And so they’ve got plenty of time for the stresses of the real world. They can become hooked on social media later on in life. They can get hooked on their device. They can do all this later, but why do we rob their childhood from them? Sure. I’ve got kids in New York public schools. I’m reasonably happy about the bans. I’m not excited about my daughter ever getting a phone. But if you were to do this straightforwardly in a legislative way, particularly the restrictions that Meta has agreed to, you would have to build out some record and you would have to do some balance of harms analysis. Here, Meta agreeing to age verification means that I, an adult, have to tell them how old I am with some tool, probably by showing them my ID. That is a big burden on me, an adult, that has nothing to do with the safety of the kids. That to me feels like it might not pass the scrutiny that the courts would provide if Meta was like, “Actually, this is too much of a burden.” How do you address that? Because the big concern here is that you’ve actually, instead of saying age verification for teens, de-anonymized the internet. The proof is the fact that Meta agreed to this in a settlement. Meta’s looking out for its corporate interest. I’m looking out for my interests as a citizen. Meta’s looking out for its ability to get more citizens like you to be engaged with it so it can make more money off of you and sell you more products. It’s in Meta’s interest to have you engage. The fact that they’re willing to step back— Right. They don’t care if I have to de-anonymize myself to look at Instagram ads for things I don’t need to buy. I’m saying I would like to be anonymous on the internet and if we put age verification everywhere, which is one of the consequences of this agreement, that every platform is going to have to start doing age verification at scale. I won’t be able to use the internet without constantly identifying myself to prove my age. I’m sure there’s a path forward that doesn’t require you to do this constantly. I’m not aware that you’d have to do it every single time you participate, every time you go to a site. I’m not aware that you’d have to do it that way. Let me find that out. I’m not going to say something without knowing that answer, but it’s an interesting point you raise. It really is. But I’m focused on the fact that we did gather data around the country to find out what is happening to our young people today. I cannot rely on parents to know how to stop this from happening, because the parents are the ones telling me, “Please do something. I don’t know how to stop this. My kid is spiraling.” One mom told me that she has her husband leave work every day at three to make sure their son, who’s being bullied in school and harassed and going to dark sites, doesn’t commit suicide when he goes home. Who wants to live with that specter? That was not the case when I was a kid, or my kids were kids. The world has changed and again, it is not a no to progress or innovation. I have thousands of examples of me inviting tech companies here. Even Micron, the largest private-sector investment in American history. 50,000 jobs are happening up in Syracuse because I went after them aggressively. They’ll be open in two years. This is extraordinary, building the memory chips that are necessary to power AI in New York state. My credentials are impeccable when it comes to inviting innovation in, but when there are areas where we need guardrails to protect individuals, I’m going to step in and do this. I feel good about this. This is a decision that we’ve made and I think it’s overwhelmingly supported by many parents. Young people someday will appreciate the fact that they were spared from this, and other people who adapt to this, this is the way it is. So much tech regulation, particularly for the last decade, has run into the First Amendment. Again, my view of it is we’ve avoided the First Amendment conversation by talking about Section 230 or other red herrings that allow us to not talk about the fact that a lot of this looks like speech regulation and expression regulation in important ways. Another good example of this, which I think will be developed, is the restriction on ghost guns in New York state. The idea is that you should not be able to 3D-print gun parts in New York state. We have a story just this week about Cody Wilson , who printed the first 3D-printed gun. He’s put out a tool to defeat the way that the law is designed to work. He calls it “Hochulization,” where he’s going to de-fingerprint the hashes of 3D-printed gun files so that whatever tool is scanning at the 3D printer level will not see that it’s a gun and print it anyway. That’s a cat and mouse game. That is a technological arms race. You can tell Cody I will get ahead of him next. I can’t always be on the forefront when I see someone intentionally thwarting a law. It is the law that you cannot have 3D-printed guns in the state of New York. And if you think it’s okay to have someone in their kitchen who may have severe mental health problems who wants to shoot up kids in your school, make a ghost gun at their kitchen table or create a munitions factory where there was none, with no regulations, no background checks, no nothing, and people broadcast that as if it’s a proper thing to do is challenge me on that, then I say go for it. Because you’re trampling in the wrong space. The question I’m asking is about implementation. I understand the desire to prevent guns from being 3D-printed and I understand that probably a lot of people would prefer that not happen. Yeah, it’s bad. It sucks. It’s wrong. But implementing that means at some point the printer itself has to know “this thing is a gun and I’m not allowed to do this.” That’s right. That is a kind of regulation on expression. We have a case for an open source e-reader that looks like a gun that people have made just to see if it will trip the software detector. Even though it’s not a gun, it looks like a gun, and there’s some line in there that is very complicated for a government regulation to address. How do you view that? Do you want the printers to literally look at things that look like guns or do you want it to be more technical, more like a database or a registry? I want to make sure that we’re getting the objective I’m looking for and I’ll figure it out. As I said, I assemble the smartest people when I make decisions, especially in the area of technology where the typical government employee is not proficient. So I’m going to use the foundation I have, but then go out there and say, “Tell me how to make sure that no one can thwart what I’m trying to do here,” and I’ll get it done. If we miss the first time, I’ll do it the second time and I’ll do it the third time because I’m not going to allow this to happen. Yes, there are other restrictions that occur. I get that. It’s not ideal, but I also didn’t think it was a smart idea for people to manufacture weapons of mass destruction at their kitchen table and kill kids. So I’m going to be the one who says no. I’d rather have the regulation that protects and prevents it. Use 3D printers for any kind of good. You can make all kinds of things with 3D printers. It’s not a ban on 3D printing. It is a use that is illegal because you cannot have a gun in the state of New York without having had a background check, having regulation, having it registered. We have all kinds of rules, which is one of the reasons why we are one of the safest states in America. Lowest gun homicide deaths in America. It’s extraordinary, because the rules are working. So not everyone loves rules. I get it. This is not the wild west. This is New York. We’re going to do it right. If there’s a theme emerging in this conversation, it’s how much can the government watch what happens on my computer and how much can it tell me what I can do with my computer? Which is maybe a 40-year-old conversation, but it’s more and more relevant over time. We’re saying we’re going to restrict how teenagers can use their phones. We’re going to restrict what you can print on a 3D printer. The flip side of that is… I would say the backlash to surveillance is bipartisan. The backlash to Flock cameras is deeply bipartisan. It’s scrambling party lines. Right. You’ve allocated budget for police departments to modernize, to install Flock cameras. How are you viewing that backlash to surveillance? I understand the anxiety around this. I truly do. But you see how it’s all the same, right? I do not have complete regulation over someone’s use of their computer. That’s an overstatement. It just is. We have a very narrow, specific purpose and a government objective to protect young people, because the companies have gone too far. If they had put these controls in place themselves, when the data was starting to show them that this is harmful to kids, [but they didn’t]. They stopped letting their own kids use this, but let everybody else be subjected to this, knowing the harms. That’s when the government has to step in and regulate business. We don’t do it as a first position. My view is more hands off. Innovate, do good things, sell your product. Great. This is called capitalism in America. A 3D printer, those are great. Until I find out they’re making guns that can kill people from them or be able to convert a Glock. Maybe it’s a legal Glock that you have registered to you, that’s great, but you can get this little piece of plastic that’s the size of a Lego and insert that and all of a sudden it can fire countless rounds per minute. Now it’s a weapon of mass destruction. The government has to be watching to an extent. Watch for excesses, but not to stifle personal use, not to stifle innovation, not to stifle the companies. When they go too far or they don’t self-regulate, using data that they have internally and ignoring it, thinking they can get away with it, that’s where we are today. I’m just connecting the dots between “I want to use my printer in some way,” “there’s a connection to the government that says yes or no,” and how people feel about technology like Flock — “I want to drive my car too fast on the highway and an automated license plate reader is going to track that and send me a ticket in the mail.” Or “cops are going to use this in ways, good and bad, and sometimes they’re going to go over the line and there’s not enough regulation,” or “I don’t want these cameras at all.” Which is what we hear from so many people in so many communities, across party lines. Actually let me read you a quote — To the extent that they’re being abused, that has to stop. Sure. The CEO of Flock recently said to a lot of people, including The Verge , that he was wrong to assume that the regulatory process would provide protections for civil liberties. He assumed that state and local governments would provide controls for Flock to prevent things like cops over-searching the database or tracking people. Tracking a lot of ex-girlfriends, for example, is a thing that we hear about cops using Flock for. That’s a pretty stunning indictment. The state is rolling out cameras to track people without the necessary controls, and the company providing the camera is saying, “Well actually you were wrong about this.” The state is not rolling these out. I give money for all kinds of technology. The localities are the ones that decide how they want that spent. I do not have a contract with Flock. That is a mischaracterization. But the money provided does not come with controls? I use the money for overtime for police. Computers in police vehicles is primarily the main focus of this. And to the extent that there are license plate readers, that’s different from the Flock cameras which are automatically transmitting information without human intervention, which is what I object to. Okay. If there’s a police officer that says, “This person is wanted for murder, let’s go get them,” you’d be happy if we went after them. But this is not just to have AI or a machine make an automatic referral of information to other agencies, whether it’s ICE or anybody else. That’s not what we’re talking about here in the state of New York. That’s not what we want to happen. If I need to tighten up regulations in that space, I will. I have no trouble looking— Can you connect that to the money that you’re allocating for this technology and say, “You have to use it this way?” Yes, we can. We can look at it. That’s an observation. That’s new information to me, that we should be having restrictions on and how they’re using it. Absolutely. What would you ask of the CEO of Flock in order to make that job easier? I’d tell him to make sure that the information can only be amassed a certain way. It has to be reviewed with human eyes to make a decision on whether or not this has to be forwarded to another law enforcement agency, the FBI or someone’s wanted list. That’s basically the purpose we want it for. I don’t want Big Brother. I don’t want unfettered surveillance of Americans that makes them anxious. It goes against the sense of liberty that we all have and deserve to have living in this country. This is not a country where the government should be monitoring everything you do, but to the extent that we have to stop crime and thwart the criminals who are always trying to take steps ahead of us, I have to get ahead of that as well, and try to manage that or else we have a lawless society. People are getting harmed and then it’s a failure of government to intercede. We’ll come to data centers, but I think data centers are doing this as well. There is some kind of realignment happening. These are not right- or left-coded issues. They’re not Democratic or Republican issues. They are scrambling that traditional very, very strong party ties that have existed for almost a decade in this country. Surveillance is one, data centers are another. Do you see that — that there’s a scrambling here? There’s nothing wrong with that. I welcome that. I have been waiting a long time for there to be more issues that people, all Americans, can galvanize behind and find some commonality. When I’m doing roundtables around the state, and I’ve done many, I don’t know if I’m talking to Democrats or Republicans. All I know is these are people worried about what’s happening in their communities with hyperscale data centers being built, making noise, causing disruption, and consuming energy. Is that driving up their own utility bills? They’re anxious about this. No, this is important. It’s an important time in our history to find that there are common interests and maybe that’s a breakthrough if you can have elected officials remind people like that: “Listen, you’re agreeing with your Republican neighbor and you’re a Democrat or vice versa.” That’s good. Greg Abbott, the governor of Texas, followed our leadership on the moratorium on hyperscale data centers — not the smaller ones for university research or educational institutions or healthcare institutions. We are very specific and these are the large-scale data centers. But to have the state of Texas follow our lead, that says something. That says something — that Americans overall are saying enough is enough. The rudest version of this question is: Doesn’t that just say that it’s an election year? No. You don’t think so? No. This only became an issue fairly recently in the state of New York. We were recently bombarded with 30 applications. That was the aha moment for me to say, “Wait a minute, if we powered all of these requests for approvals, how much power would I have left for everybody else in the state?” I’ll give one example: in upstate New York, there’s a county, St. Lawrence County. Five applications for data centers are pending right now. I said, “How much power would all those consume?” The equivalent of everything I would generate with one nuclear reactor. So I’m trying to build more nuclear power. I want to get ahead of the game and try to reduce the cost of power, make sure we never have shortages. All the work to get one nuclear reactor would be consumed by five data centers in one of my 62 counties. You expect your government to say, “Wait a minute.” If this had come up to me five years ago, I would have done it five years ago. This has nothing to do with electoral politics at all. In fact, my opponent embraces data centers. The President embraces data centers. They’re the ones on the wrong side of history on this one. If they were smart, they’d say, “You know what, the governor’s right. Let’s just stand out on this issue because our constituents are not with us on this.” This is what I mean by a realignment issue. The President does embrace the data centers. He calls them, “Money printing machines,” which I think is very funny. Unclear if he knows what actually happens at a data center. But then you have, right in Texas, a similar moratorium. We just ran a story about Republican voters in Florida , hardcore MAGA voters, people who organized the Stop the Steal rally saying they would not vote for Byron Donalds if he won the primary. He won the primary, he’s going to run on data centers. We’ll see if he adjusts his position, but that’s a realignment. And I’m wondering if the answer is just in a year’s time when your moratorium expires, it’ll be over and we’ll start building again, or if there’s something specific you’re looking for as a solution to bring construction back online. A couple of points. In one year from now, the communities in the state of New York that want to host hyperscale data centers will have far more tools at their disposal than they do today, which is what I’m trying to give them. I want them to have what I call my community investments framework. I have studied what data centers have done for communities all over America. I have a list. I know that in South Bend, Indiana, the community received $143 million of benefits. Other areas have had bonuses for teachers and supporting roads and infrastructure, energy infrastructure. I want our residents to know that their local elected officials have gotten the best deal they possibly can because right now, think about the negotiation that goes on between a small-town, maybe a part-time mayor, a small economic development staff, and they’re supposed to negotiate against a tech giant. It’s not going well. I want to help them out. Why are there tax breaks in the state of New York for a data center? They have more money than God. They don’t need tax breaks that hurt my small farmers and my small towns. This is where they’re going. They’re not coming to New York City. These are going to rural areas, generally Republican areas, which is very interesting. But also the water consumption. Are they all using the hyperloop? Are they doing something else? Do they need to make the noise they do? Do they need to be this size? I’ve asked these questions. In fact, I posed a challenge to the data companies: “You’ve created a powerful force that is changing civilization as we know it, the way we communicate, the way we work, the way we live with AI. Why don’t you ask AI how to create power that uses less energy, uses less space? Can you go vertical? Maybe you can go vertical, take up less farmland, less space, but it costs more. Well, then pay more.” They’re trying to go vertical. They’re trying to go all the way up to space. [Laughs] Maybe the whole thing should go up to space. That’s the other question. We are talking about one that’s seven miles large. Seven miles, I can’t even conceive of that. We have some already that I’ve looked at in the East Coast and they’re huge. What happens when the technology changes and they do this underwater or in space or they figure out a way to make it much smaller? Nuclear reactors can now be small modular reactors. Things change and what happens to the community when they’re left with this monstrosity left behind? You have to be thinking about this in advance. I told the people who work at the big AI labs that I was talking to you and I said, “What do you want to know?” Now I will concede they all think AI is a net good. They all think it’s going to be great. We have some people in our audience who do not agree with them, but speaking for them, they all think AI will be a net good. It will improve humanity. The question was, “What do you want the hyperscalers to give?” If you believe that AI progress will be a net good and inevitable, what is the ask that enables that development to happen? I will restate my challenge. I understand you need the power. I have harnessed AI in the state of New York, in state government in a way no other governor has. I have used AI to look at every single rule, regulation, policy, board, and commission. Has that been effective? Is that just you alone with Claude? How does that work? I don’t do it myself. [Laughs] I have smarter people than me that do. All right. Fair enough. Literally I said, “What would it take for us to look at every rule in the books? And are they smart? Are they obsolete? Are they too expensive? Are they too burdensome?” Let’s ask those questions. I like to rethink. I’m always challenging the status quo. It’s how I’m hardwired. Let’s look at the state government. People think it’s intractable. I say we can make it leaner, smarter, more efficient. And in literally a month, I had a list of thousands of recommendations, what would have taken five to 10 years for humans to do. I announced the first 50 already: we saved over a million and a half hours for New York businesses and individuals when it comes to filling out redundant forms. My first 50 out of thousands, saving millions of dollars in other areas. There was a $25 fee to take your dog hunting with you. You had to pay for a $25,000 bond to move a mobile home on a highway. Why? Get rid of that. Why does someone have to do that? A woman could not work after midnight if she was pregnant. You had to have special permission to do that. Sending information by telegraph and telegram. I just looked at this and said, “I used AI as a force of good to rethink state government.” So I’m not opposed, but I’m saying to them, “You already know what a next-generation data center looks like. It does not have to be this big. It does not have to use this much power. Figure it out now before there’s even more hostility towards you. Your public relations are dreadful by the way. No one understands what you’re trying to do and you come in like big bullies and you think you can run all over a little community, maybe you did in the early years.” They’re getting a little smarter now. They’re starting to give more community benefits, but they’ll figure it out. Let me ask you about this. You’re a politician in a campaign year. I hear so much from the AI labs that what they have is a marketing problem, that if people could only understand the benefits, if they communicated them more broadly, they would win far more hearts and minds and people would be all behind this build out. I personally disagree with that. Everybody sees AI overviews in Google all day long. A billion people have used ChatGPT. The products are known to people and the capabilities are known to people. Maybe there’s some set of very advanced capabilities like the things you’ve described you’ve done in government that would unlock even more. But I don’t think they have a marketing problem. They have an attitude problem. To some extent they have a product problem. I don’t think the products are good enough to support the asks, and these are enormous asks as you’ve been describing. How would you handle that for them? How would you say, “Look, these are big build outs, the potential benefits to humanity are high and from the government side, here’s what you actually need to say and promise to people in order to work on this productively”? It’s not that. People know the benefits. Your kid gets a bite, you’re going to take a picture and ask Claude, “Is this a tick bite or a mosquito bite? Do I need to worry about this?” The way that medicine has even been integrated into people’s lives, asking questions. It’s already being employed in a positive way for the people who want to use it in a positive way, as you’ve said. The data centers, the hyperscalers, have become the physical manifestation of people’s anxiety about the future. Think about all the young people that I literally spent years myself telling, “Go into STEM careers, kids, learn science and math. You’ll have a job forever. Oh yes, study coding and computer science. The jobs are going to be there.” Guess what? Those are the jobs that are going first. People are anxious about displacement. They’re worried. They’re not opposed to advancement and technology in the future, but where do they fit into it? Government has to be addressing that anxiety. When people see the data centers, they’re thinking, “Oh geez, that’s my job that could be gone.” [AI labs] have to do a better job addressing the concerns that people have. Don’t make a big show about laying off 10,000 people in your company and literally tell them it’s because of AI. I had people who were displaced sitting in my office. They’re told they’re gone because of AI. That was more of a shareholders’ play to show your shareholders you’re streamlining and saving money, but that’s a lot of people’s lives you just ruined. That’s what’s going on. Those are the conversations that I’m hearing in places where they’ll never see a data center, like here in New York City. Their challenge is to help people see that this is not [negative]. If they can’t prove this proposition, then they’re probably going to lose the battle for the hearts and minds. But show us the jobs that can be created. What other jobs should people be going to? When I’m told that, “81% of the jobs likely to be displaced are held by women” — Women took this long to finally make it into the workplace and in significant positions or positions where it’s administrative or legal secretaries or legal assistants, even new lawyers. All the jobs that you can think of are held by women. A woman might be the primary breadwinner. If she thinks her job’s going to be gone because of AI, she’s not going to love an AI company. She’s going to say, “Wait a minute, what about me?” They need to figure out what the AI future looks like. Tell us right now the skills that are required. What should I be teaching in schools? What should we say the state education department should be teaching? What courses should students be taking in college to prepare the next generation of workers, so they will not be in that displacement? We have a whole lot of people who are already in that vulnerable spot. The individuals just getting out of college, those who are mid-career, what are they supposed to do? I saw this personally. I’m from Buffalo. Buffalo Bills fan. I’ll put that right out here now. We haven’t talked about the stadium , but we can get there. We’ll get to the stadium. We saved the Bills. That’s all you need to know. They’re not in another state. There you go. They are the Buffalo Bills, and they weren’t going to be. But not far from there, my parents used to live in a trailer park near the steel mill. Everybody worked at the steel plant, Bethlehem Steel. It was the best job you could get. My dad worked there, my grandpa worked there, my uncles worked there. In 1982, they picked up and left town. No one thought about the workers, the 20,000 workers in my town that now just lost their livelihoods. They left. My point is that I lived through that. I will not let that happen now. That’s what people are anxious about, losing their livelihoods. I just want to connect two dots here right at the end, because I’m really happy you brought up the idea that it’s the physical manifestation of anxiety. This is a trope, I think, in the tech industry. It’s true: data centers are big, they’re noisy. You can look at them and you can say stop. But we started out talking about all the things you might want to keep people from doing on computers, or keep computers from doing to people, maybe more importantly. Again, it’s been a decade of attempts to do this. We don’t have a privacy law in this country. There are all these things that we don’t have because of the First Amendment. We were unable to overcome the First Amendment to regulate social media in some very big, important ways. You can stop a data center. The power of NIMBYism is strong in America, and the tools exist to stop it. Is this the wrong tool for the job to say we’re going to do land use and NIMBYism instead of regulating labor and employment and the future of young people more directly? There are two different dynamics here, a big difference. One is the application of AI and how it’s being utilized. I’m asking about the mechanism. I understand the goals, but it’s the mechanism that I’m really thinking about here. The mechanism of the data centers, of the power they’re creating? We might want to regulate AI to make sure there are more and better jobs, or protect women in the workplace. The mechanism that we’re using to get to that outcome is we’re going to stop the data centers until they make better promises. See, I don’t see it as one or the other. Both are occurring right now. But stopping the data centers is not my objective here. It is to make sure that they do it right for the communities that want it. There’s a big difference. Maybe the companies will negotiate in a way, or they might say, “I guess we didn’t need that much space,” or “Yeah, we figured out a way to make it not noisy at all. You won’t even know we’re there,” or “We’re going to do a better job shielding this.” Everyone talks about Loudoun County, Virginia… We have a big story about Loudoun County coming next week. You know why I know Loudoun County? Because when I said my family had to leave Buffalo because there were no jobs, guess where they went to? I’m one of six kids; four of my siblings landed in Loudoun County many years ago when it was all farmland. Now they have in the backyard of their homes these massive data centers. For a while it was like, “Wow, look at this. Our taxes can go down. We’re benefiting from this.” But do you know what? After a while, the tax abatement stopped, or the benefits stopped over a length of time. Now they’re starting to see their utility bills and property taxes go up. What they were sold years ago when they were the test case of a community that had lots of data centers, believe me, there’s buyer’s remorse. Not just for my siblings, but for many people who are saying, “You know what? We didn’t get the best deal after all. What are we doing here?” I learned from other examples around the state, around the country, around the world, and I want to make sure that what we do in New York is based on the soundest, smartest practices. We embrace AI. Do there have to be data centers? If they have to be there, are they doing it in the best way? I’m going to challenge them.I know I’m going to keep pushing them to do better. When I first became an elected official in my small town, that’s when all the tech comms came and they all wanted their own cell tower. “Everybody’s going to want their own cell phone. We have to have our own freestanding tower.” I said, “Those are ugly. I don’t want these giant cell towers in neighborhoods and everywhere. They’re horrific.” So I said to them, “Why don’t you co-locate? Can’t you all go on one tower, you and your five competitors?” “No, that’s not possible.” “Okay. Can you go on top of a water tower? Can you go on top of a tall building?” “No, no, no. We have to…” So I passed the toughest law regulating cell towers in the entire state in my small town, and I forced them to pay me for the ability. I said, “I’m going to challenge you. I’m going to get outside experts when you tell me you can’t do something, and you’re going to pay for the cost of that consultant.” They did. Guess what? They co-locate. They’re on top of water towers. My town does not have cell towers everywhere, but we were told it had to be that way because I presume it was the cheapest, the best for them, the easiest for them to just throw these up. I said, “What happens when the technology changes and you’re bouncing this off of satellites?” This was a long time ago. I said, “I don’t want to be looking at any kind of towers here.” I made them put in a bond. They had to pay money for us to be able to dismantle this and take it down, even if it’s 50 years from now. I know how to do this. I’ve done it before. And that’s what I’m trying to do for New York: use my experiences on how to manage this. We didn’t say no to cell phones. We said yes to cell phones. We say yes to AI, but in a way that the companies have to be challenged by the government to do it better because their own profit motives will let them do whatever’s cheapest and fastest for them. That’s not necessarily serving the public good. That’s what I have to protect. Governor, you’ve given us a ton of time. You’ve answered a lot of questions here. We did go fast. It’s an election year. I am very curious about this big realignment scramble. Give people your view of what to expect in this election year as surveillance, data centers, and AI scramble our traditional party lines. How do you think that’s going to play out? What is top of mind is very much the data centers nationally, and it’s fascinating to me to see that in races for Congress and governor in other states, they’re using this as a political point. I could not have foreseen that six months ago. Public opinion has shifted so quickly. But again, regardless of what happens in the election, I do think Democrats will prevail for many, many reasons. There’s so much going on, and we can get to other topics on trade wars with Canada and how it’s having an effect. You brought up the Bills. I want to talk about the NFL’s antitrust exemption. But that’s for another time. [Laughs] Can we just talk about the fact that the Buffalo Bills stayed in Buffalo? I fought hard. Look, I’m a Packers fan. What do you think the Bears should do? We got another hour on that. I actually like small-town markets. I like the Packers. I used to follow them closely. Way before you were born, I was a big AFC fan. The Bills used to play the Packers all the time. So we can talk sports anytime. But I just want to leave people with this sense. I believe that Democrats will take back the House and the Senate and position themselves to take back the White House, but we have to do it in a smart way that shows that we are attuned to the anxieties of Americans. I know that people are very anxious about their future, their jobs, how they’re going to take care of their families in a world where AI seems to be so ever-present, and it is that data center that scares them. We can do more to shape that, make sure that people understand that’s in one sense a necessary evil, but that evil doesn’t have to be as evil as it is. Make it less evil, and people will adapt and adjust and understand this. The companies are complicit in this sense of, “We can do what we want because we’re so big.” Americans, when they go to vote, want people who are going to stand up and not just roll over. They have a president and Republicans in Congress, my Republican opponent, who are rolling over trying to convince people that, “No, this is good,” when in fact you have people like me and some others who are saying, “Let’s do this smart. Let’s be thoughtful about this. I’m not going to roll over. I don’t roll over for anybody.” That’s the impact on the elections. Democrats are going to win. Governor, thank you so much for your time. Thank you for implying that I’m young. That was very nice of you. I really appreciate it. [Laughs] It’s all relative, right? Questions or comments? Hit us up at decoder@theverge.com. We really do read every email! ]]>
paragraphs: Today, I’m talking with New York Governor Kathy Hochul, and I’ll just warn you — this episode moves really fast. It’s an election year, after all, with a shocking amount of tech policy at stake, and Governor Hochul has taken strong positions on almost every major tech issue there is.

For example, Meta just reached a settlement with dozens of states, including New York, which will restrict how teens use platforms like Instagram in very specific ways. Governor Hochul is a strong supporter of those restrictions and more, as you’ll hear. But those come with a cost — widespread age verification means adults will also have to show ID to use the internet, which will essentially make it impossible to be anonymous online.

So I asked about that, and if these new restrictions amount to Meta conceding in a lawsuit that these kinds of regulations on speech might not pass First Amendment scrutiny if the governor were to try and impose them in a law.

I had similar questions about New York’s restrictions on ghost guns, which prevent 3D printers from printing gun parts. That law is already being challenged — not in courts, but by activists like Cody Wilson, who runs the largest database of 3D-printable gun files and who has started altering those files in a process he calls “Hochulization” in order to show the ban is technically toothless. I asked the governor about this, and, well, you’ll hear her challenge Cody right back.

Oh, but there’s more: We also talked about surveillance and Flock cameras, and, of course, the politics of AI and data centers in an election year. Governor Hochul signed a one-year moratorium on data center construction in July, and I wanted to know what she’s looking for when that expires to make data centers a workable proposition.

paragraphs: After an unreleased OpenAI model wreaked enough havoc to make international headlines, OpenAI delayed the development of a different unreleased model suite, Astra, in order to shore up its safety work, the company wrote Tuesday in a blog post.

In July, an unreleased OpenAI model broke out of its restricted environment, finagled its way into internet access, made it possible for AI agents to secretly conspire under the company’s nose using a secret message board, and hacked into the network of AI lab Hugging Face. The attack sparked weeks of discussion and controversy inside and outside the AI industry, and AI leaders treated it as a “warning shot” for the tech’s growing capabilities and the inadequacy of its safeguards.

OpenAI said as much in its blog post, writing that although Astra wasn’t involved in the Hugging Face attack, the company had chosen to delay “parts of Astra’s development and release while we strengthened and tested protections against cyber misuse and unauthorized model actions.” OpenAI also said that Astra was the first model it had ever designated as meeting its “ C c ritical cybersecurity capability threshold,“ meaning that it’s able to find and exploit security vulnerabilities in “many well-protected systems” without human guidance. That means it “requires stronger safeguards during development and before release,” OpenAI wrote.

OpenAI said that to prepare for Astra’s release — which the company has not yet provided a timeline for — the company trained it to “more reliably” say no to potentially harmful cyber requests and introduced new monitoring processes. These are likely part of the new safety guardrails that the company announced in a Hugging Face post-mortem last week , where it promised to better isolate models from the internet and to introduce “24/7 escalation and rapid response” for concerning incidents. (OpenAI didn’t find out about the Hugging Face attack until weeks after it occurred.)

Astra is significantly riskier than OpenAI’s current leading model, GPT-5.6 Sol, the company says, because it represents a big step forward in cybersecurity capabilities — specifically, it uses fewer tokens to do more work, and it’s better at finding security gaps and developing ways to exploit them. But the company also wrote that Astra was its “most aligned model to date” according to internal evaluations.

OpenAI also said it had developed a test inspired by the Hugging Face attack, in which it tried to entreat agents to compromise security infrastructure instead of solving a task. It said GPT-5.6 Sol took the bait in more than half of the tests, but Astra “made no such attempts.”

article.title: GTA 6 nặng đến mức PS5 Pro cũng khó đạt 60 FPS
article.summary: Thông tin này xuất hiện sau buổi trải nghiệm GTA 6 kéo dài khoảng ba giờ tại Rockstar North của YouTuber Davy Jones. Trong đó, Giám đốc phát triển Rob Nelson đã trực tiếp chơi game hơn hai giờ.
article.dek: Thông tin này xuất hiện sau buổi trải nghiệm GTA 6 kéo dài khoảng ba giờ tại Rockstar North của YouTuber Davy Jones.
article.hook: Thông tin này xuất hiện sau buổi trải nghiệm GTA 6 kéo dài khoảng ba giờ tại Rockstar North của YouTuber Davy Jones.

sections.heading: Bối cảnh: điều gì đang đổi
sections.body: Thông tin này xuất hiện sau buổi trải nghiệm GTA 6 kéo dài khoảng ba giờ tại Rockstar North của YouTuber Davy Jones. Trong đó, Giám đốc phát triển Rob Nelson đã trực tiếp chơi game hơn hai giờ. Jones cho biết trò chơi chạy ở 30 FPS trong suốt phần trình diễn.

sections.heading: Các nguồn đang khớp nhau ở đâu
sections.body: GTA 6 xây dựng thế giới mở đông đúc với nhiều hệ thống mô phỏng, tạo áp lực xử lý lớn lên phần cứng của hệ máy console.

sections.heading: Tác động thực tế với người đọc
sections.body: Khi được hỏi liệu GTA 6 có chế độ ưu tiên hiệu năng hay không, Nelson cho biết trò chơi hiện chạy ở 30 FPS và ông cần trao đổi với đội ngũ kỹ thuật để biết khả năng đạt 60 FPS khi phát hành hoặc sau đó. Rockstar vì thế chưa đưa ra bất kỳ cam kết nào về chế độ 60 FPS trên console.

sections.heading: Ai nên chú ý lúc này
sections.body: Mức 30 FPS vốn không xa lạ với game của Rockstar. GTA 5 từng giới hạn ở 30 FPS trên PS3 và PS4 trước khi phiên bản dành cho PS5 bổ sung tùy chọn 60 FPS. Tuy nhiên, GTA 6 có thể là bài toán khác khi lượng công việc mà hệ thống phải xử lý không chỉ tập trung vào chất lượng đồ họa.

sections.heading: Điều cần theo dõi tiếp
sections.body: CPU có thể là một trong những giới hạn khiến GTA 6 khó đạt tốc độ khung hình cao. Một thế giới đông NPC cùng các hệ thống giao thông, vật lý, thời tiết và AI hoạt động liên tục tạo ra lượng tính toán lớn mà CPU phải đảm nhiệm.

Apple đang nỗ lực cải thiện năng lực trí tuệ nhân tạo (AI) sau khi được cho là chậm chân hơn các đối thủ như Microsoft và Google. John Ternus và Tim Cook tại Apple Park. (Ảnh: Apple) Apple được kỳ vọng ra mắt phiên bản Siri mới sử dụng các mô hình AI Gemini của Google tại Hội nghị các nhà phát triển toàn cầu (WWDC) vào tháng 6. Bên cạnh đó, Apple được cho là đang chuẩn bị một trong những thay đổi lớn nhất đối với iPhone, với mẫu iPhone màn hình gập dự kiến ra mắt không lâu sau khi Tim Cook rời ghế CEO. Dưới thời Ternus, Apple cũng có thể trình làng kính thông minh và các sản phẩm tập trung vào AI nhằm cạnh tranh với những thiết bị AI thế hệ mới, trong đó có sản phẩm được OpenAI định hướng phát triển theo mô hình “AI-first”. Chặng đường mới của Apple dưới sự lãnh đạo của John Ternus sẽ chính thức bắt đầu từ ngày 1/9. Apple chuẩn bị sự kiện iPhone khác lạ nhất trong nhiều năm VOV.VN - Apple đã chốt ngày ra mắt iPhone mới, nhưng kế hoạch được cho là sẽ phá vỡ truyền thống giới thiệu toàn bộ dòng máy.
paragraphs: Tim Cook sẽ tiếp tục làm việc tại Apple với vai trò Chủ tịch điều hành và hỗ trợ công ty trong một số lĩnh vực, trong đó có làm việc với các nhà hoạch định chính sách trên toàn thế giới, theo thông báo của hãng “Táo khuyết”.

Trong thời gian giữ chức CEO, Tim Cook đã giám sát quá trình Apple ra mắt nhiều sản phẩm mới, trong đó có Apple Watch, AirPods và gần đây là MacBook Neo. Ông cũng đóng vai trò quan trọng trong việc đưa doanh thu mảng Dịch vụ của Apple vượt mốc 100 tỷ USD, trở thành mảng kinh doanh lớn thứ hai của công ty, chỉ sau iPhone.

CEO Tim Cook khi đến thăm Việt Nam năm 2024. (Ảnh: Mạnh Hùng) Steve Jobs tuyển Tim Cook vào Apple năm 1998 và bổ nhiệm ông làm Phó Chủ tịch điều hành phụ trách bán hàng toàn cầu năm 2002, trước khi đưa ông lên vị trí Giám đốc vận hành (COO) vào năm 2005. Năm 2011, Tim Cook kế nhiệm Steve Jobs và trở thành CEO Apple.

Trong thời gian lãnh đạo, vị CEO này tận dụng kinh nghiệm về chuỗi cung ứng để mở rộng đáng kể hoạt động kinh doanh của Apple. Vốn hóa thị trường của công ty tăng từ khoảng 350 tỷ USD lên hơn 4.000 tỷ USD, tương đương mức tăng khoảng 1.000%.
Doanh thu hàng năm của Apple tăng mạnh, từ 108 tỷ USD năm 2011 lên 416 tỷ USD năm 2025. Riêng doanh thu iPhone tăng mạnh từ 47,1 tỷ USD lên 209,6 tỷ USD trong cùng giai đoạn.
CEO Apple Tim Cook. (Ảnh: Getty) Apple Watch và AirPods cũng trở thành những sản phẩm đồng hồ thông minh và tai nghe phổ biến nhất thế giới.

draft_context.source_title: 33-hour BGP hijack of Softaculous traffic prompts security scramble
draft_context.description: Softaculous and Virtualizor customers are being urged to reset credentials and inspect their servers after a 33-hour BGP hijacking incident diverted traffic and delivered malware to a handful of installations. Softaculous makes software for the web hosting industry, while its Virtualizor control panel is used by providers and administrators to deploy and manage virtual private servers. Beginning at around 20:57 UTC on August 28, an unrelated network began announcing a block of Hetzner IP addresses used by Softaculous, diverting some traffic intended for the vendor's systems to an attacker-controlled server. German hosting provider Hetzner is one of Softaculous's upstream infrastructure providers. The affected addresses served "a number of Softaculous systems," including Virtualizor's software update endpoint and Softaculous's client and billing site. The attacker pulled off the BGP hijack by announcing a more specific IP address range than Hetzner normally advertised. Under standard BGP route selection, the more specific route took precedence wherever it was accepted. According to Softaculous, the attacker was also able to secure a valid TLS certificate from Let's Encrypt because the certificate authority's automated domain-ownership validation was routed through the hijack too. This allowed affected connections to reach the attacker's server without triggering the certificate warnings that might otherwise have alerted users. According to the vendor's timeline, the unauthorized route was initially "accepted by essentially every internet vantage point that receives it," although it flapped repeatedly rather than remaining continuously available. Softaculous said it reported the issues to Hetzner at around 08:50 UTC on August 29. The hosting provider began directly announcing the same, more-specific address range, cutting the observed diversion to almost zero for roughly 11 hours. The unauthorized announcement returned at around 20:00 UTC and was again widely accepted, beginning a second wave that lasted roughly ten hours. The route was withdrawn between 05:50 and 06:10 UTC on August 30, after which normal routing was restored globally. While either wave was active, Softaculous estimates that a given server had roughly a 72 percent chance of being on a network that routed the affected address range through the attacker. The figure is based on the proportion of RIPE routing collector peers carrying the hijacked route, not the volume of traffic intercepted, the vendor said. Anyone who logged into the Softaculous client area during the incident window is advised to reset that password immediately, as well as anywhere else it was reused. Customers who entered card details during the same window should also review their statements. Softaculous said it does not process cards on its own servers and instead uses payment gateways, but an affected session may have been diverted before reaching them. More seriously, the vendor confirmed that a malicious Virtualizor update package was delivered to a handful of installations whose update checks passed through the attacker's server. "Our product update clients did not yet cryptographically verify update packages, so a modified package would not have been rejected on that basis." Because those downloads never reached its own logs, Softaculous said it "cannot produce a definitive list" of affected installations. It is therefore telling every Virtualizor operator to treat their server as in scope for checks – not necessarily as compromised. Softaculous did not describe the malware's capabilities, but identified a systemd unit at /etc/systemd/system/java-jre-update.service as an indicator of compromise. Operators that find it are advised not to delete it immediately, but to contact the vendor so evidence can be preserved. The vendor has not identified malicious packages targeting Backuply, Softaculous, SitePad, Webuzo, or its other products, although its investigation continues. Virtualizor operators should rotate and restrict their API credentials, check for unknown SSH keys and accounts, inspect scheduled tasks and outbound connections, and regenerate client-area API keys. Softaculous is also invalidating client-area sessions created during the incident window. Softaculous did not disclose how many customers downloaded the malicious update or may have handed credentials to the attacker. It said only that the confirmed infections amounted to "a handful of servers rather than the general Virtualizor user base." ®

draft_context.source_title: I tried Sony's new ULT Tower party speakers, and they shook me to my core — here's everything you need to know about the striking new models
draft_context.description: Sony reveals 3 new party speakers: ULT Tower 5, ULT Tower 7, and ULT Tower Max ULT Tower 3, £349 (around $470 / AU$660); ULT Tower 7, £499, (approx. $680 / AU$940); ULT Max £1,299 (about $1,800 / AU$2,500) New circular woofers, multiple sound modes, 360-degree party sound Sony has revealed three new party speakers and — hurrah! — I’ve had the chance to hear them for myself. The Sony ULT Tower 5, ULT Tower 7, and ULT Tower Max look to offer almighty audio output for parties, DJ sets, or even karaoke sessions, with various ways to play and connect. These bass-conscious new speakers are built around newly developed large, circular woofers (a departure from Sony's almost rectangular X-Balanced woofer unit, typically seen across the ULT range), and according to Sony, the Max model specifically delivers the most powerful bass in the ULT Power series to date. Their bold designs — which also deviate a fair bit from previous ULT speakers — as well as their massive power outputs and broad connectivity options could make them a major rival for the likes of JBL’s PartyBox models, if the sound is right. Just how good do Sony’s new ULT speakers sound? I attended an impressive demo and I’ll reveal what I thought shortly. First, let’s run through everything I learned about Sony’s Towers, from technical specifications to nifty new features. Taking a closer look (Image credit: Sony) Let’s look closer at each of the three new ULT Tower speakers, and go through the key technical details. The ULT Tower 5 is the smallest in the new line-up, but it still packs quite the punch. It contains a 230mm woofer and two tweeters with a 300W maximum power output. Meanwhile, the ULT Tower 7 boasts a larger 280mm woofer, alongside two mid-range units, and four tweeters — two front-facing, and two rear-facing. The rear tweeters are also angled for a wider soundstage. The ULT Tower 7 has a 420W maximum power output. Finally, the ULT Tower Max is a true beast of a speaker. It has three woofers, two front-facing, one rear-facing. But it also comes with two-midrange units, and four tweeters, two of which are rear-facing. Its high-power amplifier delivers 2,150W of output, making it one of the most powerful party speakers I’ve ever encountered. I want to focus in on the woofers for a moment, because Sony were really keen to stress the changes made for the new ULT Tower models. Unlike some previous models, the new Towers have circular driver units for the woofers, rather than the ‘X-Balanced’ alternative. Sony Product Manager Mike Somerset told me: “X-Balanced is fantastic for a smaller, compact system and maximizing the surface area inside — let’s say, for a rectangular speaker unit, you know. And it also delivers a really great, impressive ‘attack’ bass. But with these, we really wanted to emphasize deep bass — and to be able to do that we’ve moved to this circular driver unit”. The speakers also have large capacity cabinets and ULT Duct tech, which is intended to help each model produce “deeper, more powerful bass with greater authority”. Do it your way (Image credit: Sony) As well as talking up the outrageous power of the ULT Towers, Sony was keen to share the impressive customizability of the speakers. That’s because there are a number of sound modes, all of which are designed for specific situations and genres. There are two ULT modes. The first, Sony says, is intended to enhance deep bass for “a rich, low frequency sound that makes your heart tremble,” with the second made to ramp things up even further for “even greater power, delivering body-shaking bass and strong sound pressure”. What’s perhaps more interesting, though, are the ‘Flat’ and ‘Live’ options. As you’d expect, Flat is designed to make a track sound as it was intended to at the mixing desk, with a more neutral, balanced approach. Live, however, is focused on delivering a more spacious sound, with a strong emphasis on vocal clarity. The speakers were tuned with the help of a number of "Hip-Hop sound creators," including producer, songwriter, and DJ, Dready, who spoke with me about the EQ adjustment process. On the Flat tuning, he said, “That’s how I would have it on a DJ set, because obviously on the controller you have the lows, mids, and highs, and we just gave it a nice blend… so, you know, when people take it, they can express themselves how they want”. Of course, if you want to personalize things even further, you can connect to the speaker with the Sony Sound Connect app and make use of the multi-band custom equalizer instead. So…how good do they sound? (Image credit: Sony) Do the ULT Tower speakers sound any good? Allow me to go through them one by one. The ULT Tower 5 arguably impressed me the most, relative to its size and cost. Sure, it leaves out the 360-degree Party Sound feature that the larger models adopt (presumably due to its lack of rear-facing drivers), but its raw power and regimented sound were hard to ignore. When listening to Luther by Kendrick Lamar and SZA, the speaker showed its considerable versatility. The vocal sample in the intro sounded textured and resonant, but then the drive and power of deep bass hit with surprising impact. Bass, though the clear star of the show, sounded controlled yet powerful, and never shrouded vocals in the mids or drums up high. We cycled between the various sound modes, and the switch between an ‘attack’ bass and deep bass mode was pretty striking. It was incredibly seamless to sift through the different modes using the ULT logo — which also happens to be a button. It’s too early to say if it’s a sure-fire hit, but for £349 (around $470 / AU$660, but these are guesstimates based on the UK pricing right now, since Sony hasn't disclosed official pricing for these regions at the time of writing), the ULT Tower 5 sounded far more impressive than some rivals I’ve tested in its price and size class. Things got even louder when we switched to the ULT Tower 7. We tried listening to Don’t Start Now by Dua Lipa, and low-frequency sounds were full-bodied, agile, and striking. Treble sounded pretty forward to me, with higher-pitched percussion seeming highly prominent, while vocals sounded clear and well-weighted in the mix. We also tried out Money by Pink Floyd, which is a great testing track for any speaker. The 360-degree sound seemed pretty effective here, and when pairing two ULT Tower 7s together in stereo mode, the spaciousness of the track was brilliantly recreated. Vocals and guitars sounded tonally accurate and well-separated, but that low-end still came through with immense drive. Finally, we hopped over to try out the behemoth that is the Sony ULT Tower Max. I’m no stranger to a rave, and the Max made me feel like I was listening to a set at my local venue. I was able to pick a track of my choosing, so I threw on Breather by Chris Stassy. And this perfectly showed off the huge sound of the ULT Tower Max. The pumping, deep bass was genuinely earth-shaking, and I could almost feel it vibrating through my soul. But spacey sounds in the mid-range still came through cleanly, and were provided plenty of room to express themselves. If you want truly mesmerizing power at a relatively moderate cost (all things considered), then the ULT Tower Max could be one to keep an eye on. We also tried pairing ten of the ULT models together, and… as you can probably imagine, the results were palpable. Auracast technology allows multiple models to chain together, and even the LED lighting syncs up across each speaker, making for an especially immersive listening experience. Final thoughts: enticing new designs and competitive pricing (Image credit: Sony) The new ULT Towers feel like Sony’s attempt to genuinely take on JBL in the party speaker arena, with the latter being particularly dominant in this field. The party speaker segment has increased in popularity as of late, and we’ve even seen new entrants like Marshall releasing its Bromley 450 and Bromley 750 speakers. But could the ULT Towers rival the likes of JBL’s Partybox models? Well, at a glance, I think they could. They offer incredible power, more than a lot of mainstream competitors, they have a new design with attractive lighting, refined sound with rounded woofers, and plenty of ways to make them sound right for you. And that’s not to mention the wide connectivity options, including Bluetooth, RCA, XLR, and USB-C. For the power and features on offer, they’re also priced relatively modestly, with the Tower 5 coming in at £349 (around $470 / AU$660), the Tower 7 at £499 (in the region of $680 / AU$940), and the ULT Max at £1,299 (about $1,800 / AU$2,500). I was also impressed to see the battery life of the speakers, with 30 hours on the ULT Tower 7 and 20 hours on the Tower 5 — that’s quite a lot of playtime given the power demands. And although features such as 360-degree audio and sound modes are exciting, Sound Field Optimization (which analyzes speaker placement and surround noise levels to offer the best sound possible) are even better. That’s something that could really set this model apart. We’ll have to test the ULT Tower models out for a bit longer to determine whether they can compete with the best, but so far, it’s fair to say that they’ve impressed me. ]]>
paragraphs: These bass-conscious new speakers are built around newly developed large, circular woofers (a departure from Sony's almost rectangular X-Balanced woofer unit, typically seen across the ULT range), and according to Sony, the Max model specifically delivers the most powerful bass in the ULT Power series to date. Their bold designs — which also deviate a fair bit from previous ULT speakers — as well as their massive power outputs and broad connectivity options could make them a major rival for the likes of JBL’s PartyBox models, if the sound is right.

Just how good do Sony’s new ULT speakers sound? I attended an impressive demo and I’ll reveal what I thought shortly. First, let’s run through everything I learned about Sony’s Towers, from technical specifications to nifty new features.
Let’s look closer at each of the three new ULT Tower speakers, and go through the key technical details.

The ULT Tower 5 is the smallest in the new line-up, but it still packs quite the punch. It contains a 230mm woofer and two tweeters with a 300W maximum power output. Meanwhile, the ULT Tower 7 boasts a larger 280mm woofer, alongside two mid-range units, and four tweeters — two front-facing, and two rear-facing. The rear tweeters are also angled for a wider soundstage. The ULT Tower 7 has a 420W maximum power output.

I heard JBL's awesome new Summit Everest speakers, and they nearly blasted me out of my seat The best Bluetooth speakers you can buy, all tested by our experts The best wireless speakers, all tested by us — from JBL, Sonos, Bose, and more Finally, the ULT Tower Max is a true beast of a speaker. It has three woofers, two front-facing, one rear-facing. But it also comes with two-midrange units, and four tweeters, two of which are rear-facing. Its high-power amplifier delivers 2,150W of output, making it one of the most powerful party speakers I’ve ever encountered.

I want to focus in on the woofers for a moment, because Sony were really keen to stress the changes made for the new ULT Tower models. Unlike some previous models, the new Towers have circular driver units for the woofers, rather than the ‘X-Balanced’ alternative.
